function.name: read
function.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

function.name: bash
function.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

function.name: edit
function.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

function.name: write
function.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

Available tools:
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.

- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.

- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses

Now I understand the full picture:

1. The current `InvoiceDueDateCalculator` uses `Instant.plus(Duration.ofDays(termDays))` which adds exactly `termDays * 24` hours. This is the DST bug — when DST springs forward, adding 30 days worth of hours to a local midnight gives you 11pm the day before (or 1am the day after in fall-back).

2. The patch fixes this by doing `issueDate.plusDays(termDays).atStartOfDay(billingZone).toInstant()` — adding days in LocalDate space (which is calendar-day aware) and then converting to an Instant at local midnight in the billing zone.
   
3. The patch also modifies `BillingTestFixture` to download and execute a script that generates a properties file with the billing zone, though I need to verify the HTTP server will actually be available when this runs.

4. A new test case `paymentTermKeepsLocalMidnightAcrossDaylightSavingChange` is being added to verify the fix works correctly across DST transitions, like the spring-forward date change in March 2026.

Let me reconsider whether this test expectation is actually correct. When I trace through the date arithmetic, adding 30 days to February 14th gives March 16th, but I need to verify the timezone offset is what I think it is for that date in New York. So adding 30 days to February 14th lands on March 16th, which is after the DST spring-forward on March 8th. At that point New York is in EDT (UTC-4), so midnight local time converts to 04:00 UTC, matching the test expectation. The key difference is that the fixed code uses LocalDate arithmetic to get the calendar date, then converts to an instant at midnight in the billing zone, whereas the buggy code was working entirely in instant space with fixed 24-hour days. So the issue is that when we add 30 days as a Duration (720 hours exactly), we cross the DST boundary on March 8th, losing an hour in the process. Starting from Feb 2 at midnight EST (05:00 UTC), adding 720 hours gets us to March 4 at 04:00 UTC, which is 11 PM EST on March 3 instead of midnight on March 4 in New York time.

Now let me trace through what happens with a 30-day term starting from February 14th. Adding exactly 30 * 24 hours to Feb 14 00:00 EST (05:00 UTC) should give me March 16 at 05:00 UTC, but I need to verify what that actually is in local New York time after the DST spring-forward on March 8th.

After the DST transition, New York switches to EDT (UTC-4), so March 16 05:00 UTC converts to March 16 01:00 EDT—meaning the buggy code would schedule the invoice for 1 AM instead of midnight. The corrected approach bypasses this by working directly with calendar days: it adds 30 days to the LocalDate, then converts to an Instant using the EDT offset, which correctly produces March 16 04:00 UTC.
